summary: Of 16 models, five reproduce their reference well (Greek Slave, Watherston and Brogden vase, Elkington jewel cabinet, tea service, obelisk shaft), five are good objects that need a fused background deleted or a part rebuilt (piano, canopy chair, urn stand, balloon-back chair, elephant), five are starting meshes only (boulder pile, balustrade, working-class home, tower, Centenary model), and one (Brompton Boilers) does not reproduce its reference. The deciding factor was not the object but the crop: every model cut out of a crowded or lit scene dragged part of the scene into the mesh.

rows: Contrapposto stance, head turn, the draped post and the round base all line up with the print.
Hair knot, the chain at the wrists and the folds of the drapery are kept; the surface reads as marble.
No background or support from the dark studio plate came through.
The back is anatomically coherent but invented; the print shows only the front.
1.65 m is an estimate for a life-size marble, not a measurement.
fig-52_greek-slave.good_for: an archival proxy for the statue's front, and a reasonable base for retopology.
next: Check the 1.65 m against a catalogued height for the statue.
Retopologise before any engine use; 1.46 million triangles is not a game asset.
fig-52_greek-slave.riff: This is the one where it just works: stance, drapery, chain and base are all there. The back is a guess, and a good one.

rows: Statue on the lid, hexagonal drum, flared foot and pinnacles in the right order and proportion.
Figure niches and the foot's seated figures are kept; fine ornament (swags, rope bands) is softened to bumps.
All pinnacles and the four visible figure groups are present.
The drum's far faces are invented; they continue the same figures plausibly.
unnumbered_watherston-brogden-vase.good_for: an archival proxy for the front; the ornament is impressionistic.
next: Compare the far faces against another engraving of the vase if one exists.
Re-render at a closer camera to judge how much ornament survived.
unnumbered_watherston-brogden-vase.riff: A hard object, a lot of figures, and the structure survives; the fine ornament is the casualty.

rows: Pagoda-style blue roof, projecting wings, lion finial and base all match.
Two framed portraits, the central statuette, two caryatids and the enamel roundels are present.
The finial group is simplified, and the portraits are only faint paintings: it is not the same pair of faces.
Gilt, silver and blue read correctly; the plate is coloured, so tone is indicative only.
The back repeats the front composition with different portraits; that is invention.
fig-54_elkington-jewel-cabinet.good_for: an archival proxy for the front.
next: Check the portraits against the catalogue description rather than the generated texture.
Remove the invented back panel if the model is shown from behind.
fig-54_elkington-jewel-cabinet.riff: Layout is right, parts are right; the portraits are paint, not portraits, and the back is a copy of the front.

rows: All seven pieces are present and separate: bowl, jug, teapot, two cups, two saucers.
The animal-head spout and lid knop on the teapot read correctly.
The pieces sit loose on a floor instead of on the two shelves of the photograph.
The photograph is monochrome, so the off-white is an assumption.
Cup interiors and saucer undersides are invented.
fig-03_tea-service.good_for: an archival proxy for the shapes; the arrangement is not the photograph's.
next: Place the pieces on shelves in Blender if the arrangement matters.
Generate each piece separately for cleaner meshes.
fig-03_tea-service.riff: Every piece is there and the teapot's animal head survives; the shelving does not.

rows: Tall tapered shaft with a broken top, the same taper and edge as the print.
Weathered yellow stone with a vertical grain.
A rough boulder stump is fused onto the foot; the print hides the real base behind boulders.
A slab edge from the left of the crop shows at the foot of the model.
5.5 m was set against standing visitors, which stand nearer the camera.
fig-24a_obelisk.good_for: an archival proxy for the shaft; the foot is invented.
next: Crop the shaft only, above the boulders, and regenerate.
Check the height against the known obelisk if the exhibit is identified.
fig-24a_obelisk.riff: The shaft is right; the foot is whatever the boulders left behind.

rows: Bell-topped urn on a flared three-footed pedestal with two bowls, as in the print.
Gilt reliefs on the foot and the fluted bowls are kept.
A tall flat wall panel with chair details is fused behind the stand.
The back of the panel is a blank slab, so the object has no real back.
fig-31c_gilt-urn-stand.good_for: a good front once the panel is deleted.
next: Delete the fused panel in Blender and check what remains.
Regenerate from a crop with the background painted out.
fig-31c_gilt-urn-stand.riff: The urn is exactly what the print shows, standing in front of a wall that is not part of it.

rows: Balloon back, shaped seat and cabriole legs match the print.
The price card on the seat is carried over.
A flat backing board with part of a gilt frame is fused behind the chair.
The board's back is a blank brown slab.
fig-31d_balloon-back-chair.good_for: a good chair once the board is deleted.
next: Delete the backing board and check the chair's rear legs.
Regenerate from a crop with the background painted out.
fig-31d_balloon-back-chair.riff: The chair is right, with a board behind it that was a wall in the print.

rows: Keyboard, music sheet, stool and scroll feet are present.
The inlay on the case is simplified; the heavy ornament of the print is smoother.
The standing man from the crop edge is fused to the left of the piano as a full figure, with a slab behind him.
The case looks lower and wider than the print's tall upright, partly because of the fused slab.
The back is a plain panelled box, invented.
fig-31a_inlaid-piano-and-stool.good_for: usable after deleting the figure and the slab.
next: Delete the man and the slab, then re-measure the piano against the 1.4 m estimate.
Regenerate from a crop that excludes the man.
fig-31a_inlaid-piano-and-stool.riff: The piano is there; so is the man leaning on it, which the print does not intend.

rows: The hooded, tufted chair with gilt edge reads, but the seat is shallow and the hood sweeps less than the print.
Tufting, gilt trim and tassels are kept.
A curtain column and small props (a drum, a footstool) are fused beside and in front of the chair.
The back is a smooth blank shell.
fig-31b_tufted-canopy-chair.good_for: usable after separating the chair from the curtain and props.
next: Select the chair alone in Blender and delete the rest.
Regenerate from a crop with the curtain painted out.
fig-31b_tufted-canopy-chair.riff: The chair's upholstery is nailed, but the curtain and floor clutter came with it.

rows: Elephant, tusks, trunk, head cloth, tassels and the howdah platform are present.
The howdah canopy is a solid helmet shape instead of an open arched canopy on slim pillars.
Two visitors from the crop are fused at the elephant's feet.
The embroidered caparison and its cross panel are kept.
The far side of the elephant and canopy are invented.
fig-27_indian-elephant-howdah.good_for: usable after rebuilding the canopy and removing the visitors.
next: Rebuild the canopy by hand as an open frame.
Regenerate from a crop that cuts above the visitors.
fig-27_indian-elephant-howdah.riff: A beautiful elephant under a canopy that has been filled in like a helmet.

rows: A heap of rough blocks, but boxier and flatter than the four big rounded boulders in the print.
Block count and arrangement differ from the print.
A flat green slab and boxy slabs from the background are fused to the back of the heap.
The heap stands on a flat brown disc.
fig-24b_boulder-pile.good_for: usable after deleting the slabs and the disc; not faithful to the arrangement.
next: Delete the slabs and disc, then compare again.
Regenerate from a tighter crop of the pile alone.
fig-24b_boulder-pile.riff: Reads as stone, but it is a different heap.

rows: The scrolled cartouche openwork on the diagonal front face is well kept.
The model is a box: a wall block, a staircase wedge, a hat and gilt knobs are fused around a diagonal panel.
The 3 m target is applied to the box, so the balustrade is smaller than stated.
fig-31e_cast-iron-balustrade.good_for: the front face only; it needs manual isolation before any other use.
next: Cut the diagonal panel out of the box in Blender.
The balustrade is a flat angled panel, which a single-image generator handles badly: model it by hand as a flat openwork panel.
fig-31e_cast-iron-balustrade.riff: The ironwork is lovely; the cube it came in is not.

rows: The facade with its central porch, gables and chimneys matches; the long side wings are plausible.
Flat grey cards float above the roof; visitors from the print are fused into the base.
A raised stepped plinth appears where the print has a low wall and a gate.
The rear and the sides are invented.
fig-33_model-working-class-home.good_for: a starting mesh for the facade.
next: Delete the floating cards and figures, then rebuild the base.
Regenerate with a second view of the building.
fig-33_model-working-class-home.riff: The facade is recognisable; the roof carries a few sheets of cardboard that the print never had.

rows: The shaft with its stacked tiers, clock stage and flag matches the engraving.
Tier divisions are kept; the arched building at the foot is reduced to a small block.
The ground and trees are baked into a flat white slab at the base.
304.8 m comes from the printed 1000 ft and is the one scale here with a basis.
fig-63_tower-conversion-design.good_for: a starting mesh for the shaft, once the slab is deleted.
next: Delete the slab and rebuild the base as the Crystal Palace nave end.
Check the tier count against the engraving.
fig-63_tower-conversion-design.riff: A thousand-foot tower that stands on a paper tablecloth.

rows: A barrel-vault canopy over a raised platform with balustrade is the right idea.
The glazed vault and the open ironwork come out solid and muddy.
Visitors are fused inside and an extra building mass sits behind.
The 6 m depth is an estimate; the dimensions are driven by the extra mass.
fig-73_centenary-model.good_for: a starting mesh for the vault and platform; not for the glazing.
next: Rebuild the vault ribs and glazing by hand.
Regenerate from a crop without the visitors.
fig-73_centenary-model.riff: The idea is right; the glass is not glass.

rows: A very long arcaded building collapses into a compact L-shaped mass.
Two domes and an arcaded front are present, but the dome count and the arcade rhythm differ.
A flat brown billboard slab is fused behind the domes.
The plan behind the facade is entirely invented.
fig-72_brompton-boilers.good_for: not usable as a likeness; proportions are wrong.
next: Build the facade by hand from the print's bay rhythm.
Do not feed an oblique view of a long building to a single-image generator.
fig-72_brompton-boilers.riff: A long street front became a little L-shaped box; one oblique view cannot give a plan.

pattern: Every failure that cost likeness came from one of three causes. (1) The crop was not clean: walls, boards, curtains, figures and ground planes were fused into the mesh (fig 24b, 27, 31a-e, 33, 63, 72). (2) Open structure came out solid (the elephant canopy, the Centenary vault). (3) The reference could not support the claim: a long building seen at an angle (fig 72) and the back of every object. The successes (3, 52, 54, the vase, the obelisk shaft) were isolated objects against a plain or dark ground. So the cheapest improvement is upstream: paint the background out of the crop, or give the generator a second view, before generating. Triangle count and file size were no help: all 16 are about 1.4 million triangles and none is watertight.
